hints: Focus on how strongly the halide ion can reduce concentrated sulfuric acid, iodide is a much stronger reducing agent than chloride.
Remember that chloride only gives steamy HCl fumes, while iodide reduces sulfur from +6 all the way down to sulfur dioxide, sulfur and even H2S.
Link the silver halide colours to ammonia solubility, AgCl dissolves to a colourless solution but AgI stays as a yellow solid even in concentrated ammonia.
walkthrough:
**Reaction with concentrated H2SO4**

Think of concentrated sulfuric acid as both an acid and an oxidiser. Chloride is a weak reducing agent, so it only does the acid-base step.

$$\text{NaCl(s) + H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(l)} \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_4\text{(s) + HCl(g)}$$

**Why iodide goes further**

Iodide is a powerful reducing agent. It first makes HI, then HI reduces the sulfur(VI) to lower oxidation states.

$$\text{8HI + H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{4I}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{S + 4H}_2\text{O}$$ 
So for NaI, both $\text{I}_2$ (purple vapour) and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ (rotten egg smell) are genuine products, plus $\text{SO}_2$ and S.

**Silver nitrate then concentrated ammonia test**

Both halides give a silver halide precipitate at first, but the colours and ammonia behaviour are different.

$$\text{Ag}^+\text{(aq) + Cl}^-\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{AgCl(s, white)}$$ 
$$\text{Ag}^+\text{(aq) + I}^-\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{AgI(s, yellow)}$$

**Dissolving in concentrated NH3**

AgCl dissolves readily in dilute and concentrated $\text{NH}_3$ to give the colourless complex $[\text{Ag(NH}_3)_2]^+$. AgI is insoluble even in concentrated $\text{NH}_3$ and stays as a yellow precipitate. So NaCl ends as colourless solution, NaI ends as yellow precipitate.

options.A: The second half is right for NaCl, AgCl does dissolve to a colourless solution, but the first half is wrong. Chloride cannot reduce concentrated H2SO4 to Cl2, it only forms HCl white fumes.
options.B: Both parts are wrong for NaCl. H2S is never formed from chloride because Cl- is too weak a reducing agent. Also the white AgCl precipitate dissolves in concentrated NH3, so you would not still see a white precipitate.
options.C: This is fully correct for NaI. I- is strong enough to reduce H2SO4 down to H2S (as well as I2, SO2 and S). With AgNO3 it gives yellow AgI which is insoluble even in concentrated NH3, so a yellow precipitate remains.
options.D: The first half is possible for NaI, since I2 is indeed formed, but the second half is wrong. AgI is yellow and does not dissolve in concentrated NH3, so you never get a colourless solution from NaI.
